report:
Conclusion: whole-body vibration (WBV) should **not** be considered proven to prevent fractures in people with osteoporosis. Some trials/meta-analyses report modest bone-density or balance/falls signals—especially with high-frequency, low-magnitude, higher cumulative-dose protocols—but fracture reduction is unproven and studies are heterogeneous. A BMJ Open systematic review specifically examined fracture/fall outcomes in adults ≥50 and did not establish a clear fracture-prevention benefit: https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/7/12/e018342. Cochrane’s review of WBV for preventing/treating osteoporosis remains the key caution that evidence is limited/insufficient for firm recommendations: https://www.cochrane.org/CD008417/MUSKEL_whole-body-vibration-for-preventing-and-treating-osteoporosis. A 2022 update suggests BMD effects may occur under certain protocols, but BMD is a surrogate and does not equal fewer fractures: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00198-022-06556-y. The Royal Osteoporosis Society summarizes the practical point: research is unclear whether vibration therapy reduces broken-bone risk, and most studies are not in people with osteoporosis: https://theros.org.uk/information-and-support/treatments-and-medicines/complementary-therapies-for-bone-health/vibration-therapy/.

Bottom line: if used, WBV should be an adjunct for selected patients who can tolerate it—not a replacement for proven fracture-risk reduction: osteoporosis medications when indicated, adequate calcium/vitamin D, weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, and clinician-guided monitoring.
